responses: After our committee discussions, my final position is that we should allocate the $5 million AI transition budget as follows: 35% to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Employee Support, 15% to Data Infrastructure, and 5% to Innovation Lab. I landed on this balance because while competitors are seeing efficiency gains from automation and Riverton has clear room to improve manufacturing processes, we can’t overlook the human element of this transition—investing in reskilling and transition assistance ensures our employees aren’t left behind, which will ultimately make the automation efforts more successful long-term. The data infrastructure piece is important for foundational support, but we don’t need to overprioritize it right now, and the innovation lab can be smaller initially since our immediate focus should be on implementing practical, impactful changes rather than speculative new products. This allocation strikes a balance between capturing near-term efficiency gains, supporting our most valuable asset (our employees), and building the necessary technical foundation without stretching the budget too thin on unproven experimentation.

For Riverton Industries’ $5 million AI transition budget, I would recommend a 35% allocation to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 15% to Employee Support, and 5% to Innovation Lab. The largest share for automation makes sense because industry benchmarks show Riverton has room to improve manufacturing efficiency, and competitors are already seeing gains from AI-powered processes and robotic automation—this will drive immediate operational cost savings and competitiveness. Pairing this with a significant workforce training investment ensures employees have the AI literacy and reskilling needed to transition into new roles created by automation, rather than being displaced, which mitigates the risk of talent gaps and maintains employee morale. Allocating 20% to data infrastructure is critical because the planning team notes that companies with strong tech infrastructure adapted faster to AI changes, and reliable data systems are foundational for both automation and future innovation. The smaller 15% for employee support addresses transition assistance and mental health needs to support staff through the change, while the 5% for innovation lab keeps a small portion for experimenting with new AI products, ensuring the company doesn’t fall behind on long-term product development without diverting resources from the immediate, high-impact needs of automation, training, and infrastructure.

When explaining my recommended budget allocation for Riverton Industries’ $5 million AI transition to someone not on the committee, I’d say I landed on 35% for Automation, 25% for Workforce Training, 15% for Employee Support, 15% for Data Infrastructure, and 10% for Innovation Lab. I prioritized automation first because our competitors are already seeing efficiency gains, and our manufacturing processes have clear room to improve—this is where we’ll start seeing tangible returns to fund other areas. I paired that with a large chunk for workforce training because we can’t just implement AI without making sure our employees have the skills to work alongside it, not against it, and I wanted to set aside enough for hands-on reskilling and AI literacy courses. Employee support was important to me too, because any transition will create uncertainty, so having career counseling and mental health resources will help people feel secure through the change, which keeps morale and productivity high. I allocated a smaller portion to data infrastructure because the benchmark says companies that get that right early adapt faster, but I didn’t want to overspend there before we have clear use cases from automation. Finally, the innovation lab got the smallest slice because we need to focus on implementing what’s proven first before experimenting with new AI products, though I wanted to leave a little room to explore future opportunities that could grow the business long-term.

After our committee discussions, my final position is that we should allocate the $5 million AI transition budget as follows: 35% to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 15% to Employee Support, and 5% to Innovation Lab. I arrived at this allocation by weighing the data points about competitors’ efficiency gains and Riverton’s room for manufacturing improvement, which made a significant investment in automation critical to remaining competitive, while also recognizing that without proper workforce training and updated data infrastructure, those automation investments would not deliver their full potential. The smaller allocation to Employee Support reflects our need to address transition needs but not at the cost of core operational investments, and the minimal Innovation Lab funding acknowledges that our immediate priority is adapting existing AI tools rather than developing entirely new products right now. I was persuaded by the argument that automation without training would leave our team members unprepared to work alongside new systems, and that outdated data infrastructure would create bottlenecks for any AI implementation, leading me to prioritize those areas alongside automation.

I would recommend allocating the $5 million budget as follows: 35% to Data Infrastructure, 25% to Automation, 20% to Workforce Training, 15% to Employee Support, and 5% to Innovation Lab. The data shows that companies with strong data infrastructure adapted faster to AI transitions, so prioritizing this foundational area ensures our systems can support all other AI initiatives securely and effectively, which is critical given cybersecurity risks in manufacturing. Allocating a significant portion to automation aligns with competitor efficiency gains and our room for process improvement, while workforce training is essential to help employees transition rather than be displaced—paired with targeted employee support to address mental health and career needs, this balances technological progress with our people-focused responsibilities. Finally, a smaller investment in innovation lab lets us explore new AI products without diverting resources from the core transition that will improve our current operations and support our team.

The data infrastructure is the backbone that makes all the other AI work possible, so we can’t skimp on that, and the small innovation lab budget lets us test new ideas without risking too much of the main funds.
